name: Gaia
tagline: The Earth herself, who armed her son against his father.
story: She bore Uranus, the sky, and with him the Titans. When Uranus kept their children hidden inside her, she gave Cronus a sickle.

name: Uranus
role: The Sky, first ruler of the world
tagline: The first father, and the first to be overthrown.
story: Husband of Gaia and father of the Titans. He kept his children from the light until Cronus castrated him.

name: Nyx
tagline: Night, mother of retribution.
story: In Hesiod she bore Nemesis and many other dark powers, without a father.

name: Cronus
tagline: Swallowed his children to keep his throne.
story: Son of Uranus and Gaia. He castrated his father and took his place. Warned that a son would overthrow him, he swallowed his children as they were born, until Rhea hid Zeus and gave him a stone instead.

name: Rhea
tagline: Fed her husband a stone to save her son.
story: Wife of Cronus. To save her youngest son, Zeus, she wrapped a stone in swaddling clothes and gave it to Cronus to swallow.

name: Oceanus
role: The river that circles the world
tagline: Father of three thousand daughters.
story: A Titan, son of Uranus and Gaia. With Tethys he fathered the rivers and the Oceanids.

name: Tethys
tagline: Mother of the rivers.
story: Wife of Oceanus and mother of the rivers and the Oceanids. In Homer, she and Oceanus raised Hera.

name: Coeus
tagline: A Titan remembered for his daughters.
story: Son of Uranus and Gaia. With his sister Phoebe he fathered Leto and Asteria.

name: Crius
tagline: The quietest of the Titans, known only through his sons.
story: Son of Uranus and Gaia. With Eurybia, a daughter of the Sea, he fathered Astraeus, Pallas and Perses.

name: Phoebe
tagline: Grandmother of Apollo and Artemis.
story: Daughter of Uranus and Gaia, wife of Coeus and mother of Leto and Asteria.

name: Hyperion
tagline: ‘The one who goes above’: father of the Sun, the Moon and the Dawn.
story: Son of Uranus and Gaia. With his sister Theia he fathered Helios, Selene and Eos.
versions: In Homer, Hyperion is often a name of the Sun himself: Helios Hyperion.

name: Theia
tagline: Mother of every light in the sky.
story: Daughter of Uranus and Gaia, wife of her brother Hyperion. Pindar calls her ‘Theia of many names’, the mother of the Sun, who gives gold its shine.
versions: The Homeric Hymn to Helios names Hyperion’s wife Euryphaessa, ‘wide-shining’, not Theia.

name: Iapetus
tagline: Every one of his sons crossed Zeus, and paid for it.
story: Son of Uranus and Gaia. In Homer he sits with Cronus in Tartarus, far below the earth.
versions: Hesiod gives him the Oceanid Clymene as wife; Apollodorus, the Oceanid Asia.

name: Themis
tagline: Zeus’s second wife, who gave birth to Order, Justice and Peace.
story: A daughter of Gaia and Uranus. In Hesiod she was Zeus’s second wife, after Metis, and bore him the Horae and the Moirai.
versions: In Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound, Themis and Gaia are one goddess under two names, and she is Prometheus’s mother. In Hesiod his mother is the Oceanid Clymene.

name: Mnemosyne
tagline: Nine nights with Zeus, nine daughters.
story: A daughter of Gaia and Uranus. Zeus lay with her for nine nights in Pieria, and when a year had passed she bore the nine Muses.

name: Atlas
role: Titan who holds up the sky
tagline: Holds up the sky, forever.
story: Son of the Titan Iapetus. Zeus condemned him to hold up the sky at the ends of the earth. Father of Maia.

name: Prometheus
tagline: Stole fire for mortals, and was chained up for it.
story: He tricked Zeus over the share of a sacrifice, then stole fire back for mortals in a fennel stalk. Zeus chained him and sent an eagle to eat his liver, which grew again each night, until Heracles shot the bird.
versions: Hesiod: the son of Iapetus and Clymene. Apollodorus: of Iapetus and Asia. In Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound his mother is Themis, who is also Gaia. Aeschylus chains him to a crag at the edge of the world; Apollodorus, on the Caucasus.

name: Epimetheus
tagline: ‘Afterthought’, who took the gift his brother warned him against.
story: Prometheus told him never to accept a gift from Zeus. He accepted Pandora, the first woman, and with her came every evil.

name: Menoetius
tagline: Too proud: Zeus struck him with a thunderbolt.
story: Son of Iapetus, brother of Atlas and Prometheus. For his arrogance and overbearing strength, Zeus hurled him down into the dark with a thunderbolt.

name: Helios
tagline: Sees everything, and once turned back in horror.
story: Son of Hyperion and Theia. He drives his chariot across the sky each day and sees all that happens on earth. When Atreus and Thyestes fought over the throne of Mycenae, he turned his course back towards the dawn.
versions: In the Homeric Hymn to Helios his mother is Euryphaessa; in Pindar, Theia. Homer often calls him Hyperion.

name: Selene
tagline: Sister of the Sun, who drives the night sky.
story: Daughter of Hyperion and Theia. She drives her chariot across the night sky.
versions: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes she is the daughter of Pallas, son of Megamedes.

name: Eos
tagline: Rosy-fingered, and always falling in love with mortals.
story: Daughter of Hyperion and Theia. Each morning she rises before her brother the Sun. With Astraeus she bore the winds and the stars.

name: Astraeus
tagline: Married the Dawn and fathered the winds.
story: Son of Crius and Eurybia. With Eos he fathered the winds, Zephyrus, Boreas and Notus, and the stars.

name: Pallas
tagline: His children stand beside Zeus’s throne.
story: Son of Crius and Eurybia. With the Oceanid Styx he fathered Zelus, Nike, Cratos and Bia: Rivalry, Victory, Power and Force, who never leave Zeus’s side.

name: Perses
tagline: Father of Hecate.
story: Son of Crius and Eurybia, ‘outstanding in wisdom’, says Hesiod. He married Asteria, and she bore Hecate.

name: Asteria
tagline: Leapt into the sea rather than be caught by Zeus.
story: Daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, wife of Perses and mother of Hecate. Pursued by Zeus, she turned into a quail and threw herself into the sea, and became an island: Ortygia, ‘Quail Island’, later Delos, where her sister Leto gave birth.

transformation.text: Became a quail, then an island

name: Erinyes
tagline: Born of a father’s blood, they hunt down whoever spills a kinsman’s.
story: When Cronus cut down his father, drops of Uranus’s blood fell on the Earth, and she bore the Erinyes. They pursue those who kill their own kin. They drove Orestes across Greece until a court in Athens acquitted him.
members_note: Apollodorus names three. In Aeschylus they come on stage as a whole chorus, unnamed.
versions: In Hesiod and Apollodorus, Gaia bore them from Uranus’s blood. In Aeschylus’s Eumenides they are the daughters of Night.

name: Hestia
tagline: The eldest, who stayed by the fire.
story: Eldest daughter of Cronus and Rhea: the first to be swallowed and the last to be released. She vowed to remain a virgin.

name: Demeter
tagline: Lost her daughter to the underworld.
story: Daughter of Cronus and Rhea, mother of Persephone by Zeus. When Hades carried off her daughter, she searched the whole earth. In Hyginus, she ate the shoulder of Pelops at Tantalus’s feast.

name: Hades
tagline: Stole a bride from the world above.
story: Son of Cronus and Rhea. With Zeus’s consent he carried off Persephone to rule the dead beside him.

name: Poseidon
tagline: Loved Pelops and carried him to Olympus.
story: Son of Cronus and Rhea, brother of Zeus, lord of the sea. In Pindar he fell in love with the boy Pelops and carried him off to Olympus.

name: Hera
tagline: Married to Zeus, and at war with his lovers.
story: Daughter of Cronus and Rhea, sister and wife of Zeus, mother of Ares and Hephaestus. She pursued Zeus’s lovers and their children.

name: Metis
tagline: Swallowed whole by her husband.
story: An Oceanid, Zeus’s first wife in Hesiod. Warned that her son would rule, Zeus swallowed her while she was pregnant, and Athena was born from his head.

name: Leto
tagline: Insulted by Niobe, avenged by her children.
story: Daughter of Coeus and Phoebe. She bore Apollo and Artemis to Zeus. When Niobe boasted of having more children than she did, Leto’s twins killed them.

name: Maia
tagline: Mother of the trickster god.
story: Daughter of Atlas. In a cave on Mount Cyllene she bore Zeus a son, Hermes.

name: Pleiades
tagline: Seven sisters, set among the stars.
story: Daughters of Atlas and the Oceanid Pleione. Three of them bore sons to Zeus: Maia, Electra and Taygete. They became the stars that still carry their name.

members.name: Sterope
members.note: in Apollodorus Oenomaus’s wife; in later writers his mother

members.name: Merope
members.note: the one who married a mortal, Sisyphus

members_note: Maia is drawn on her own.
versions: Hesiod calls them simply ‘born of Atlas’; Apollodorus and Ovid name their mother, Pleione. Ovid says only six can be seen, because Merope hides, ashamed that she married a mortal. Others say it was Electra who hid her face, so as not to watch Troy fall.

name: Dione
role: Goddess, mother of Aphrodite in Homer
tagline: Aphrodite’s mother, or no one’s.
story: In Homer she comforts her wounded daughter Aphrodite.
versions: Homer and Apollodorus make her the mother of Aphrodite by Zeus; Hesiod has Aphrodite born from the sea. Hesiod counts Dione among the Oceanids, Apollodorus among the Titans.

name: Oceanids
tagline: Three thousand sisters, scattered over the earth.
story: Daughters of Oceanus and Tethys: nymphs of springs, rivers and the sea. Hesiod names forty-one of them. The eldest, Styx, gave her name to the water by which the gods swear.

members.name: Styx
members.note: the eldest of them; the gods swear by her water

members.name: Dione
members.note: an Oceanid in Hesiod; in Homer, Aphrodite’s mother

members.name: Eurynome
members.note: mother of the Charites, by Zeus

members.name: Clymene
members.note: in Hesiod, mother of Atlas and Prometheus

members_note: Hesiod names forty-one; these are the ones the tree meets. Metis and Dione are drawn on their own.

name: Semele
tagline: Asked to see a god in his glory, and died of it.
story: Daughter of Cadmus, the founder of Thebes. Zeus loved her. Tricked by Hera, she asked him to come to her as he came to Hera, and died when he arrived in thunder and lightning. Zeus saved her unborn son, Dionysus.
versions: Apollodorus: she died of fright at his thunder and lightning. Ovid: she was burned by his fire. In Ovid, Hera tricks her disguised as her old nurse, Beroe.

immortal.text: Made a goddess. Dionysus brings her up from Hades, and in Apollodorus she rises to heaven as Thyone

name: Athena
tagline: Born fully armed from her father’s head.
story: Daughter of Zeus. Zeus swallowed her mother Metis, and Athena sprang from his head.
versions: Homer calls her simply Zeus’s daughter. Hesiod and Apollodorus tell of Metis and the birth from his head.

name: Apollo
role: God of prophecy, music and plague
tagline: Killed Niobe’s sons for his mother’s honour.
story: Son of Zeus and Leto, twin of Artemis. With his sister he shot down the children of Niobe.

name: Aphrodite
tagline: Born from the sea, or from Zeus.
story: Wife of Hephaestus and lover of Ares.
versions: Hesiod: she rose from the sea foam around the severed flesh of Uranus. Homer and Apollodorus: daughter of Zeus and Dione.

name: Hephaestus
role: God of fire and the forge
tagline: The lame smith who caught his wife in a net.
story: Son of Hera. In the Odyssey he caught Aphrodite and Ares together in a net of fine chains.
versions: Hesiod: Hera bore him alone, without a father. Homer seems to make him a son of Zeus and Hera, and Apollodorus reads him so, while himself telling the Hesiodic version. The Odyssey makes Aphrodite his wife; Hesiod gives him Aglaea, youngest of the Graces.

name: Dionysus
tagline: Born twice: from his mother, then from his father’s thigh.
story: Son of Zeus and the Theban princess Semele. When his mother burned, Zeus sewed the unborn child into his thigh until he was ready to be born.

name: Persephone
tagline: Carried off to rule the dead.
story: Daughter of Zeus and Demeter. Hades seized her as she picked flowers, with Zeus’s leave, and made her queen of the underworld. She spends a third of each year with him and the rest with her mother.
versions: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter and Hesiod make her Demeter’s daughter. Apollodorus names her mother as Styx, though his story of the abduction has Demeter searching for her.

name: Ares
tagline: The war god, grandfather of a doomed bride.
story: Father of King Oenomaus in Apollodorus and Pausanias.

art.title: Ludovisi Ares
art.meta: Roman copy, 2nd century AD, of a Greek original

name: Hermes
tagline: His son’s murder starts the curse.
story: Father of Myrtilus, whose dying curse fell on the house of Pelops. In Apollodorus he carried the advice from Zeus that won Atreus back the throne.

art.title: Hermes and the Infant Dionysus
art.meta: attributed to Praxiteles; some scholars date it later

name: Plouto
tagline: A nymph at the root of the tree.
story: Later authors name her as the mother of Tantalus by Zeus.

name: Zeus
tagline: Where it all begins.
story: Father of Tantalus. In some versions, also father of Helen and of one or both of the Dioscuri.

art.title: Artemision Bronze, Zeus or Poseidon

name: Nemesis
tagline: Retribution herself, and perhaps Helen’s mother.
story: In the Cypria she fled Zeus through many shapes and became the mother of Helen. In Apollodorus she became a goose, and Zeus a swan.

transformation.text: Many shapes, fleeing Zeus; in Apollodorus a goose

art.title: Head of the Nemesis of Rhamnous

name: Artemis
tagline: She demanded a daughter for a deer.
story: Agamemnon killed her sacred deer and boasted of it. Her price was Iphigenia.

art.title: Diana of Versailles
art.meta: Roman copy of a Greek bronze attributed to Leochares

name: Hecate
tagline: The one goddess Zeus honoured above all.
story: Daughter of Perses and Asteria. Hesiod praises her at length: Zeus gave her a share of the earth, the sea and the sky. Later writers made her the goddess of crossroads, of the night and of witchcraft.
versions: In the Catalogue of Women, as Pausanias reports, Iphigenia does not die at Aulis: by the will of Artemis she becomes Hecate.

name: Muses
tagline: Daughters of Memory, who taught a shepherd to sing.
story: Hesiod met them on Mount Helicon while he tended sheep. They gave him a laurel staff and breathed a poet’s voice into him. Homer calls on them at the start of both his epics.

members.name: Calliope
members.note: the first of them all, in Hesiod

members_note: Hesiod names all nine. Each Muse’s own art (Calliope epic, Clio history and the rest) was settled much later.
versions: Homer once speaks of nine, singing at Achilles’ funeral. Pausanias reports that the first to honour them on Helicon, the sons of Aloeus, knew only three: Melete, Mneme and Aoede, Practice, Memory and Song.

name: Horae
tagline: Order, Justice and Peace, who keep the gates of heaven.
story: Daughters of Zeus and Themis. In Homer they keep the cloud gates of Olympus, rolling the clouds back for the gods’ chariots.
members_note: Hesiod and Apollodorus name these three; other writers give other names and numbers.

name: Moirai
tagline: Daughters of Night, or of Zeus: not even the poets could settle who made fate.
story: They give each mortal a share of good and evil at birth. Clotho spins the thread of a life, Lachesis allots it, and Atropos, who cannot be turned, cuts it.
versions: Hesiod gives them two births: as daughters of Night alone, and later as daughters of Zeus and Themis. Apollodorus follows the second; Hyginus makes them children of Night and Erebus. Homer mostly speaks of a single Moira.

name: Charites
tagline: Three sisters of beauty and delight, one of them married to the smith.
story: Daughters of Zeus and the Oceanid Eurynome. In Hesiod the youngest, Aglaea, married Hephaestus; in the Iliad his wife is called simply Charis, a Grace.
members_note: Hesiod and Apollodorus name these three.
versions: Pausanias records other counts and names: the Spartans honoured two, Cleta and Phaenna, and the Athenians two, Auxo and Hegemone.

name: Oenomaus
tagline: Killed every suitor who raced for his daughter.
story: Son of Ares. He raced his daughter’s suitors in chariots and killed every one who lost.
versions: Most writers make him a son of Ares. Pausanias, sceptical of divine fathers, also reports a mortal one, Alxion.

art.title: East pediment, Temple of Zeus at Olympia

name: Tantalus
tagline: Served his son to the gods.
story: Tested the gods by serving them his own son, Pelops, and was punished forever in the underworld.
versions: Most sources make Zeus his father and the nymph Plouto his mother; one ancient commentary on Euripides names the mountain god Tmolus instead. Homer punishes him with endless hunger and thirst; Pindar and Euripides hang a great stone over his head. Pindar even rejects the cannibal feast: in his telling Tantalus stole the gods’ nectar and ambrosia.

art.title: Tantalus, from The Four Disgracers
art.meta: Hendrick Goltzius after Cornelis van Haarlem, 1588
art.where: engraving; this impression at the Metropolitan Museum of Art

name: Cadmus
tagline: Sowed a dragon’s teeth and reaped a city.
story: Sent to find his sister Europa, he founded Thebes instead. He killed the serpent of Ares that guarded the spring and, on Athena’s advice, sowed its teeth. Armed men sprang up and killed each other until five were left. The gods came to his wedding with Harmonia. In old age the two of them were turned into serpents.
versions: Euripides: Dionysus foretells that he and Harmonia will become serpents, lead a barbarian army against Greece, and be brought by Ares to the land of the blessed. Apollodorus: Zeus sends them as serpents to the Elysian Fields. Ovid: Cadmus asks to become a serpent, and Harmonia follows him.

transformation.text: A serpent, with Harmonia, at the end of his life

immortal.text: Sent with Harmonia to the Isles of the Blessed, or the Elysian Fields

name: Harmonia
role: Daughter of Ares and Aphrodite, queen of Thebes
tagline: Love and War’s daughter, married to a mortal with a necklace that ruined every woman who wore it after her.
story: The daughter of Ares and Aphrodite. The gods came down to her wedding with Cadmus, and the Muses sang. She bore Ino, Semele, Agave, Autonoe and Polydorus. Her wedding necklace, made by Hephaestus, brought ruin to the women who wore it after her.
versions: Apollodorus: Cadmus gives her a robe and the necklace made by Hephaestus; he adds that Pherecydes had it come from Europa, who had it from Zeus. A Samothracian tradition, outside the sources this tree follows, makes her a daughter of Zeus and Electra.

transformation.text: A serpent, with Cadmus, at the end of her life

name: Polydorus
tagline: The quiet son between a founder and a curse.
story: The only son of Cadmus and Harmonia. He ruled Thebes and was the father of Labdacus.

name: Labdacus
tagline: Founder of a doomed line.
story: Grandson of Cadmus and father of Laius. The Labdacids take their name from him.

name: Agave
tagline: Tore her son apart and carried his head home in triumph.
story: Daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, wife of Echion, one of the men sown from the serpent’s teeth. She said her sister Semele had lied about Zeus. Dionysus drove her mad, and on Mount Cithaeron she and the women of Thebes tore her son Pentheus apart.
versions: Euripides: she takes Pentheus for a young lion. Ovid: for a boar. Apollodorus: for a wild beast.

name: Pentheus
tagline: Locked up a god and was torn apart for it.
story: Son of Agave and grandson of Cadmus, who gave him the throne. He forbade the rites of Dionysus and jailed the god’s followers. Lured to Mount Cithaeron to spy on the women, he was torn apart by his mother and her sisters.
versions: Euripides: Dionysus dresses him as a maenad and leads him to the mountain. Ovid: he goes to the mountain himself, in a rage.

name: Myrtilus
tagline: Betrayed his master, was betrayed in turn, and cursed them all.
story: Son of Hermes. He sabotaged his master’s chariot so Pelops could win. Thrown into the sea by Pelops, he cursed his line as he fell, and the Myrtoan Sea is named after him.

art.title: East pediment, Temple of Zeus at Olympia
art.meta: c. 460 BC; a kneeling figure is often identified as Myrtilus

name: Hippodamia
tagline: The prize of a rigged race.
story: Daughter of Oenomaus, wife of Pelops, mother of Atreus and Thyestes.

art.title: East pediment, Temple of Zeus at Olympia

name: Pelops
role: King who gave his name to the Peloponnese
tagline: Won his bride by cheating, then drowned his accomplice.
story: Son of Tantalus, restored to life by the gods after the terrible feast. He won Hippodamia by treachery and killed Myrtilus. The curse on the house begins here.
versions: Pindar rejects the terrible feast: in his telling Poseidon fell in love with the boy and carried him off to Olympus.

art.title: East pediment, Temple of Zeus at Olympia

name: Niobe
tagline: Boasted of her children and lost every one.
story: Daughter of Tantalus. She boasted to Leto of her many children; Apollo and Artemis killed them, and Niobe turned to stone on Mount Sipylus, a rock that still weeps.

art.title: Niobe with Her Younger Daughter
art.meta: Roman, first half of the 2nd century AD

art.title: Apollo and Diana Attacking the Children of Niobe

name: Jocasta
tagline: Wife of Laius, then of her own son.
story: Mother and wife of Oedipus. When the truth came out, she hanged herself.
versions: Homer calls her Epicaste. In the lost epic Oedipodeia, as Pausanias reports, Oedipus’s four children are born to a second wife, Euryganeia.

name: Laius
tagline: Abducted a prince and brought a curse on Thebes.
story: Abducted Chrysippus, son of Pelops, and was cursed for it. Warned that his son would kill him, he had the infant Oedipus exposed.
versions: The abduction and Pelops’s curse appear only in later sources, probably after Euripides’ lost play Chrysippus.

art.title: The Murder of Laius by Oedipus

name: Chrysippus
tagline: The stolen son who links two cursed houses.
story: Abducted as a youth by Laius of Thebes, whom Pelops then cursed.

name: Atreus
tagline: Served his brother a dinner of his own children.
story: On learning of his wife’s affair with his brother, he killed the sons of Thyestes and served them to their father at a feast.

name: Aerope
tagline: Gave her husband’s golden lamb to his brother.
story: Granddaughter of Minos. Wife of Atreus, unfaithful to him with Thyestes.

name: Thyestes
tagline: Seduced his brother’s wife and ate his own sons.
story: After the terrible feast he cursed the house of Atreus. Father of Aegisthus.

name: Tyndareus
tagline: A mortal king raising the children of Zeus.
story: Husband of Leda and mortal father of Clytemnestra and Castor.

name: Leda
tagline: Visited by a swan.
story: Wife of Tyndareus. Zeus came to her in the form of a swan.

art.title: Leda and the Swan

name: Theseus
tagline: Kidnapped Helen when she was a girl.
story: In Stesichorus, Iphigenia is their daughter.

art.title: Theseus and the Minotaur

name: Oedipus
tagline: Killed his father, married his mother.
story: Exposed as a baby, he grew up in Corinth, killed Laius at a crossroads and married Jocasta. Learning the truth, he blinded himself and cursed his sons.
versions: Homer: Epicaste hangs herself and Oedipus goes on ruling Thebes. Sophocles: he blinds himself and goes into exile. The epic Thebaid already has him curse his sons, over his father’s golden cup and a slighting cut of meat.

art.title: Oedipus and the Sphinx
Oedipus and Antigone, or The Plague of Thebes

name: Pleisthenes
tagline: The forgotten father, written out of Homer.
story: In the Catalogue of Women and Apollodorus, the true father of Agamemnon and Menelaus. He died young, and Atreus raised his sons.
versions: Homer never mentions him. Tzetzes, citing Hesiod and Aeschylus, makes him a son of Atreus and Aerope.

name: Agamemnon
role: King of Mycenae, leader of the Greeks at Troy
tagline: Sacrificed his daughter to win a war.
story: Murdered in his own house on his return from Troy.
versions: Homer: son of Atreus. The Catalogue of Women, Aeschylus (as reported by Tzetzes) and Apollodorus: son of Pleisthenes, raised by Atreus. His mother is Aerope, or in one report Cleolla.

art.title: The Mask of Agamemnon
art.meta: gold funerary mask, c. 1550–1500 BC, centuries older than any Trojan War

name: Menelaus
tagline: The husband left behind.
story: Husband of Helen. Her flight with Paris sparked the Trojan War.
versions: As with Agamemnon: son of Atreus or of Pleisthenes, depending on the source.

immortal.text: Not fated to die: sent to the Elysian Fields as Zeus’s son-in-law

art.title: The Pasquino Group, Menelaus Supporting the Body of Patroclus
art.meta: Roman copy; some scholars read it as Ajax with Achilles

name: Pelopia
tagline: Bore a son to avenge her father.
story: In Hyginus, mother of Aegisthus, the son born to avenge Thyestes on Atreus.

name: Clytemnestra
tagline: Waited ten years to kill her husband.
story: She avenged Iphigenia by killing Agamemnon, and died at her son’s hand.
versions: Homer: an accomplice, while Aegisthus strikes the blow. Aeschylus: she kills Agamemnon herself.

art.title: Clytemnestra
Clytemnestra Hesitates before Killing the Sleeping Agamemnon

name: Helen
tagline: The face that launched a thousand ships.
story: She left her husband Menelaus and sailed with Paris to Troy.
versions: Homer: daughter of Zeus, her mother unnamed. Euripides: daughter of Zeus and Leda, hatched from an egg. The Cypria and Pausanias: her mother is Nemesis, and Leda only nursed her. Apollodorus tells both, and in his Nemesis version a shepherd brings the egg to Leda.

immortal.text: Made a goddess, honoured with her brothers; or taken with Menelaus to the Elysian Fields; or married to Achilles on the White Island

art.title: Helen of Troy
art.where: De Morgan Collection, shown at Wightwick Manor

art.title: The Abduction of Helen

name: Paris
tagline: Chose Aphrodite and took Helen.
story: Son of Priam and Hecuba. Before he was born, his mother dreamed she gave birth to a firebrand, so the baby was left to die on Mount Ida, where a herdsman raised him. Asked to judge which goddess was the most beautiful, he chose Aphrodite, who promised him Helen. He carried her off from Sparta, and so began the Trojan War. He killed Achilles with an arrow, and died by an arrow of Philoctetes.
versions: Homer calls him Alexander as often as Paris, and mentions the Judgement only once, in the last book of the Iliad.

art.title: The Judgement of Paris

name: Castor
tagline: The mortal twin.
story: Usually a son of Tyndareus, though some sources make both twins sons of Zeus.

immortal.text: Shares his brother’s immortality: the twins live on alternate days

art.title: The San Ildefonso Group
art.meta: Roman, c. 10 BC; read as Castor and Pollux, or as Orestes and Pylades

name: Polydeuces
tagline: Shared his immortality with his brother.
story: The immortal twin, who gave up half his immortality to share it with Castor.
versions: The Odyssey: both twins are sons of Tyndareus. Hesiod and the Homeric Hymns: both are sons of Zeus. Pindar and Apollodorus: only Polydeuces is the son of Zeus, and so immortal.

immortal.text: Immortal, and shared it with Castor: the twins live on alternate days

art.title: The Rape of the Daughters of Leucippus
art.meta: Peter Paul Rubens with Jan Wildens, c. 1618

name: Eteocles
tagline: Refused to share the throne.
story: Son of Oedipus. He kept Thebes from his brother, and they killed each other in single combat.

name: Polynices
tagline: Marched an army against his own city.
story: Son of Oedipus. Exiled, he led the Seven against Thebes and died by his brother’s hand.

art.title: Antigone in Front of the Dead Polyneikes

name: Antigone
tagline: Buried her brother against the king’s law.
story: She guided her blind father in exile, then buried Polynices in defiance of Creon and was condemned to death.

art.title: Antigone in Front of the Dead Polyneikes
Oedipus and Antigone, or The Plague of Thebes

name: Ismene
tagline: The sister who stayed silent.
story: She would not join Antigone in defying Creon.

name: Pylades
tagline: The friend who never left.
story: Orestes’s cousin and his companion in exile and revenge. He marries Electra.

art.title: Pylades and Orestes Brought as Victims before Iphigenia
The San Ildefonso Group
art.meta: Roman, c. 10 BC; the Prado reads it as Orestes and Pylades

name: Electra
tagline: Lived for her father’s revenge.
story: She helped her brother avenge their father.
versions: Homer names Agamemnon’s daughters as Chrysothemis, Laodice and Iphianassa. The Catalogue of Women already has Electra, beside Iphimede. The lyric poet Xanthus says Electra was first called Laodice.

art.title: Electra at the Tomb of Agamemnon

name: Chrysothemis
tagline: The sister who would not take sides.
story: In Sophocles she tried to talk Electra out of revenge.

name: Iphigenia
tagline: The daughter on the altar.
story: Sacrificed to Artemis so the Greek fleet could sail for Troy.
versions: Homer does not know her. The Cypria: Artemis swaps her for a deer, carries her to the Taurians and makes her immortal. Catalogue of Women: as Iphimede she becomes Hecate by the will of Artemis. Aeschylus: she dies at the altar. Euripides: Artemis carries her to the land of the Taurians. Stesichorus, via Pausanias: she is the daughter of Theseus and Helen, raised by Clytemnestra.

transformation.text: Replaced by a deer, or made immortal

immortal.text: Made immortal by Artemis, or made Hecate

art.title: The Sacrifice of Iphigenia
The Sacrifice of Iphigenia, wall painting
art.meta: 1st century AD, from the House of the Tragic Poet, Pompeii

name: Orestes
tagline: Killed his mother and ended the curse.
story: Hunted by the Furies after the killing, he was tried in Athens and acquitted.

art.title: Orestes Pursued by the Furies (The Remorse of Orestes)
Pylades and Orestes Brought as Victims before Iphigenia

name: Aegisthus
tagline: Born to kill, and he did.
story: Clytemnestra’s lover. He killed Atreus, then Agamemnon.
versions: Homer: Aegisthus kills Agamemnon. Aeschylus: Clytemnestra strikes the blow. Apollodorus and Hyginus: Aegisthus is the son of Thyestes by his own daughter, whom Hyginus names Pelopia.

art.title: Clytemnestra Hesitates before Killing the Sleeping Agamemnon
art.meta: Pierre-Narcisse Guérin, 1817; Aegisthus urges her on

name: Hermione
tagline: Promised to two men.
story: Promised to Orestes, given to Neoptolemus, and finally married to Orestes after all.

name: Hebe
tagline: Poured the gods’ nectar, then married the strongest man alive.
story: Daughter of Zeus and Hera, and the gods’ cupbearer. When Heracles was taken up to Olympus, she became his wife.

name: Acrisius
tagline: Locked his daughter away to cheat a prophecy, and was killed by it anyway.
story: An oracle told him his daughter’s son would kill him. He shut Danaë in a bronze chamber, then cast her and her baby out to sea in a chest. Years later, at funeral games in Larissa, a discus thrown by Perseus struck him dead.
versions: Apollodorus: the discus hits his foot. Ovid tells another story: Acrisius, driven out by his brother Proetus, is restored when Perseus turns Proetus to stone.

name: Danaë
tagline: Visited by Zeus as a shower of gold.
story: Her father shut her away from all men. Zeus came to her as a shower of gold, and she bore Perseus. Mother and child were set adrift in a chest and washed up on Seriphos.

name: Perseus
tagline: Brought back a head that turned men to stone.
story: Son of Zeus and Danaë. Sent to fetch the Gorgon’s head, he cut it off with help from Athena and Hermes, without looking at her. On the way home he freed Andromeda from a sea monster and married her. He killed his grandfather by accident, as the oracle had said.
versions: Apollodorus: ashamed to rule Argos after the death, he exchanged it for Tiryns. Ovid: Medusa’s head turns Phineus and his men to stone at the wedding feast.

name: Andromeda
tagline: Chained to a rock for her mother’s boast.
story: Her mother Cassiopeia boasted she was lovelier than the Nereids, and Poseidon sent a flood and a sea monster. Andromeda was chained to a rock as its prey. Perseus killed the monster and married her.

name: Medusa
tagline: The only mortal of the three Gorgons.
story: One of the three Gorgon sisters, and the only one who could die. Her gaze turned men to stone. Perseus cut off her head while she slept, and the winged horse Pegasus and Chrysaor sprang from her neck, her sons by Poseidon.
versions: Hesiod: Poseidon lay with her in a soft meadow. Ovid: she was a beautiful girl, raped by Neptune in Minerva’s temple, and the goddess turned her hair to snakes. Apollodorus: some say she was beheaded for vying with Athena in beauty.

transformation.text: From a beautiful girl to a Gorgon with snakes for hair, by Athena’s anger

name: Alcaeus
tagline: Grandfather of Heracles, whose first name was Alcides after him.
story: A son of Perseus and Andromeda, and the father of Amphitryon.
versions: Apollodorus gives three possible mothers for Amphitryon: Astydamia, daughter of Pelops; Laonome; or Hipponome.

name: Electryon
tagline: Killed by his son-in-law, over cattle.
story: A son of Perseus, king of Mycenae and father of Alcmene. He promised her to Amphitryon, who killed him over a herd of cattle.
versions: Hesiod: Amphitryon killed him in anger over cattle. Apollodorus: by accident, when a club thrown at a cow bounced off its horns.

name: Sthenelus
tagline: Took the throne his nephew lost.
story: A son of Perseus. After Amphitryon killed Electryon, Sthenelus banished him and took Mycenae. He married Nicippe, a daughter of Pelops; their son Eurystheus was born first, so Hera made him master of Heracles.

name: Nicippe
tagline: Her son was born early, so Heracles would serve him.
story: A daughter of Pelops and the wife of Sthenelus. Hera hurried her labour so that Eurystheus was born before Heracles, and so became his master.
versions: Apollodorus names her Nicippe; in the Iliad she is only “the noble wife of Sthenelus”.

name: Amphitryon
tagline: Came home to find Zeus had been there first.
story: Son of Alcaeus. After killing Electryon he fled to Thebes with Alcmene, and Creon purified him. While he was away at war, Zeus came to Alcmene in his likeness; Amphitryon came home the same night. She bore twins: Heracles to Zeus, Iphicles to him.

name: Alcmene
tagline: Bore twins by two fathers on one night.
story: Daughter of Electryon and wife of Amphitryon. Zeus came to her in her husband’s shape and made one night as long as three. She bore Heracles, the son of Zeus, and Iphicles, the son of Amphitryon. Hera held back her labour so that Eurystheus would be born first.

name: Menoeceus
tagline: Father of a queen and a regent.
story: A Theban of the line of the Sown Men, and the father of Jocasta and Creon.
versions: Euripides gives the name also to Creon’s son, who killed himself to save Thebes in the war of the Seven.

name: Creon
tagline: Ruled Thebes between its kings, and buried his niece alive.
story: Brother of Jocasta. He ruled Thebes whenever it had no king: he purified Amphitryon, gave his daughter Megara to Heracles, and offered the throne and his sister to whoever solved the Sphinx’s riddle. After the brothers killed each other, he forbade the burial of Polynices and walled up Antigone for defying him.

name: Eurystheus
tagline: The weaker man who gave the stronger one his labours.
story: Son of Sthenelus and grandson of Perseus. Hera made sure he was born first, so that he and not Heracles would rule. He set Heracles his labours, and hid in a bronze jar when Heracles brought back the boar of Erymanthus.
versions: His death: Apollodorus has Hyllus kill him, and Alcmene gouge out his eyes; Pindar, Iolaus; in Euripides’ Children of Heracles, he is taken alive and put to death at Alcmene’s demand.

name: Heracles
tagline: Earned his place among the gods the hard way.
story: Son of Zeus and Alcmene, and hated by Hera from before his birth. He strangled her serpents in his cradle. Driven mad by her, he killed his own children, and served Eurystheus for twelve labours to atone. He died in agony in a poisoned robe his wife sent him, and was taken up to Olympus, where he married Hebe.
versions: Apollodorus: Eurystheus set ten labours, then refused to count two, the Hydra (Iolaus had helped) and the stables of Augeas (Heracles had asked for pay), so there were twelve. Euripides: the madness comes after the labours, not before, and he kills Megara too.

immortal.text: Taken up from his pyre to Olympus, married to Hebe; only his shade is seen in Hades

name: Iphicles
tagline: The mortal twin, a night younger.
story: Son of Amphitryon and Alcmene, born with Heracles but fathered by a mortal, a night younger. When Hera sent serpents to the cradle, Heracles strangled them. His son Iolaus was Heracles’s charioteer.
versions: Apollodorus reports Pherecydes’s version: Amphitryon put the serpents in the cradle himself, to learn which twin was his; Iphicles fled and Heracles stood his ground.

name: Megara
tagline: Her husband killed their children in a fit of madness.
story: Daughter of Creon, given to Heracles for freeing Thebes. Hera sent him mad, and he killed their children.
versions: Euripides and Hyginus: he kills Megara too. Apollodorus: he kills only the children, and later gives Megara to his nephew Iolaus.

name: Deianira
tagline: Killed her husband with a love charm.
story: Princess of Calydon, won by Heracles in a wrestling match with the river Achelous. The dying centaur Nessus gave her his blood as a love charm. When Heracles brought home a younger woman, Iole, she smeared it on a robe and sent it to him. It burned him to death, and she killed herself.

name: Circe
tagline: Turned men into pigs, and cleansed her niece of a brother’s blood.
story: Daughter of Helios and the Oceanid Perse, and sister of Aeetes. On her island she turned Odysseus’s men into swine. When Jason and Medea fled Colchis with Absyrtus’s blood on their hands, she purified them.

name: Aeolus
tagline: Father of kings who thought themselves gods.
story: King in Thessaly, and father of a great house: Cretheus, Athamas, Salmoneus and Sisyphus were his sons.
versions: Not the keeper of the winds in the Odyssey, who is another Aeolus, son of Hippotes.

name: Salmoneus
tagline: Played at being Zeus, and got a real thunderbolt.
story: A son of Aeolus. He called himself Zeus, dragged bronze kettles behind his chariot for thunder and threw torches for lightning. Zeus struck him down and wiped out his city.

name: Cretheus
tagline: Grandfather of Jason.
story: A son of Aeolus and founder of Iolcus. He married his niece Tyro and raised her sons by Poseidon with his own.

name: Tyro
tagline: Loved a river; Poseidon came in its shape.
story: Daughter of Salmoneus. She loved the river Enipeus, and Poseidon took its form to lie with her. She bore him the twins Pelias and Neleus, then married Cretheus and bore Aeson, Pheres and Amythaon.

name: Athamas
tagline: Nearly sacrificed one son and shot another.
story: A son of Aeolus. By Nephele he had Phrixus and Helle; then he married Ino, Cadmus’s daughter, who plotted against them. Later, driven mad by Hera for sheltering the infant Dionysus, he killed his own son Learchus.

name: Nephele
tagline: Sent a golden ram to save her children.
story: First wife of Athamas and mother of Phrixus and Helle. When Ino plotted to have Phrixus sacrificed, Nephele sent a ram with a golden fleece to carry the children away.

name: Ino
tagline: A stepmother who became a sea goddess.
story: Daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, and second wife of Athamas. She parched the seed corn so the crops failed, and bribed the messengers to say the god wanted Phrixus sacrificed. She nursed her nephew Dionysus; Hera drove her mad, and she leapt into the sea with her son Melicertes.

immortal.text: Became Leucothea, the White Goddess of the sea, who saved Odysseus from drowning

name: Phrixus
tagline: His stepmother’s plot gave the world the Golden Fleece.
story: Son of Athamas and Nephele. About to be sacrificed, he escaped on a flying ram with a golden fleece. He reached Colchis, sacrificed the ram to Zeus and gave its fleece to King Aeetes, who hung it on an oak.

name: Helle
tagline: Fell from the ram and gave her name to a sea.
story: Daughter of Athamas and Nephele. Fleeing with her brother on the golden ram, she fell into the sea, which was named the Hellespont after her.

name: Pelias
tagline: Sent his nephew for the fleece, and was boiled by his daughters.
story: Son of Poseidon and Tyro, twin of Neleus. He took Iolcus from his half-brother Aeson. Warned to beware a man with one sandal, he sent Jason to fetch the Golden Fleece. Medea tricked his daughters into cutting him up and boiling him, promising to make him young again.

name: Aeson
tagline: Lost his throne to his brother, and his life too.
story: Son of Cretheus and Tyro, and father of Jason.
versions: Apollodorus: while Jason was away, Pelias meant to kill him; he asked to die by his own hand and drank bull’s blood. Ovid: he lived to see Jason return, and Medea made him young again.

name: Aeetes
tagline: Promised the fleece, then set a task meant to kill.
story: Son of Helios and the Oceanid Perse, brother of Circe, and father of Medea by the Oceanid Idyia. He kept the Golden Fleece Phrixus gave him. He told Jason to yoke his fire-breathing bulls and sow a dragon’s teeth before he could have it.

name: Creon of Corinth
tagline: Gave his daughter to Jason, and burned with her.
story: King of Corinth, where Jason and Medea lived in exile. He married his daughter to Jason and ordered Medea out of the city. He died trying to save his daughter from Medea’s poisoned robe.
versions: Not Creon of Thebes, the brother of Jocasta.

name: Jason
tagline: Won the fleece with a witch’s help, then left her for a princess.
story: Son of Aeson. He came to Iolcus wearing one sandal, and his uncle Pelias sent him to fetch the Golden Fleece. He sailed on the Argo with the best of the heroes, among them Heracles, Castor and Polydeuces, and Orpheus. In Colchis Aeetes’s daughter Medea fell in love with him and helped him with every task. Years later, in Corinth, he left her to marry the king’s daughter.
versions: Hesiod: he brings Medea home to Iolcus and they have a son, Medeus, raised by Chiron; no betrayal. Euripides: the betrayal and revenge in Corinth.

name: Medea
tagline: Killed for love, then killed for revenge.
story: Daughter of Aeetes, granddaughter of Helios, and devoted to Hecate. She fell in love with Jason and gave him a salve against her father’s fire-breathing bulls, lulled the serpent that guarded the fleece, and fled with him. To stop her father’s pursuit she killed her brother Absyrtus. In Iolcus she had Pelias killed by his own daughters. In Corinth, when Jason left her, she sent his bride a poisoned robe, killed her own children, and escaped in the chariot of the Sun.
versions: Who killed the children: Euripides makes Medea kill them herself; in older tellings the Corinthians do. Hesiod gives her and Jason a son, Medeus, and no tragedy.

name: Absyrtus
tagline: Cut to pieces to slow his father down.
story: Son of Aeetes. Medea took him with her when she fled. As their father’s ship gained on them, she killed him and scattered the pieces, so that Aeetes stopped to gather his son.
versions: Euripides: she killed him at home, by the hearth, before she fled. Hyginus: Aeetes sent him after the Argo, and Jason killed him. Ovid sets the killing at Tomis, which he says took its name from the cutting.

name: Glauce
tagline: A wedding gift set her on fire.
story: Daughter of Creon of Corinth, and Jason’s new bride. Medea sent her a robe and a golden crown as gifts; when she put them on, they burned her and her father to death.
versions: Apollodorus calls her Glauce; in Euripides she is only the princess. Hyginus calls her Creusa: a poisoned golden crown burns her, Creon and Jason with her.

name: Hypsipyle
tagline: Hid her father when the women killed all the men.
story: Queen of Lemnos, the island where the women killed every man. She alone saved her father, Thoas. When the Argo put in, she took Jason as her lover and bore him sons, one of them Euneus.

name: Orpheus
tagline: Out-sang the Sirens.
story: Son of the Muse Calliope. His lyre moved trees and stones. He sailed with the Argonauts, and when they passed the Sirens he played so loudly that his crewmates heard him instead.
versions: Apollodorus: son of Calliope and Oeagrus. Pindar seems to make him a son of Apollo. Pausanias denies that his mother was a Muse.

name: Dardanus
tagline: The son Zeus loved best of all his mortal sons.
story: Son of Zeus. He founded Dardania on the slopes of Mount Ida, before there was a city on the plain. Of all the sons that mortal women bore him, Zeus loved Dardanus best.
versions: Homer names only his father. Hesiod, Apollodorus and Ovid make his mother the Pleiad Electra, daughter of Atlas.

name: Erichthonius
tagline: The richest of men, with three thousand mares.
story: Son of Dardanus, and the richest of mortal men. Three thousand mares grazed his marshes. The North Wind loved them, came to them as a dark-maned stallion, and sired twelve foals that ran over the ears of the corn without breaking them.
versions: Not Erichthonius of Athens.

name: Tros
tagline: Gave the Trojans his name, and lost a son to Zeus.
story: Son of Erichthonius, and the king the Trojans are named after. When Zeus carried off his son Ganymede, Tros mourned him without end, so Zeus sent him the finest horses under the sun.

name: Ilus
tagline: Built the city on the plain.
story: Son of Tros. He founded Ilium, the city on the plain also called Troy. His tomb stood out on the plain, where the armies later fought around it.
versions: Apollodorus: he followed a dappled cow, and founded the city where it lay down.

name: Assaracus
tagline: Grandfather of Anchises.
story: Son of Tros, and brother of Ilus and Ganymede. His line, through Capys and Anchises, led to Aeneas.

name: Ganymede
tagline: Too beautiful to stay on earth.
story: Son of Tros, and the most beautiful of mortals. The gods caught him up to Olympus to pour wine for Zeus, and live among the immortals.
versions: Homer: the gods took him for his beauty. Ovid: Zeus became an eagle to carry him off.

immortal.text: Made deathless and ageless, to pour the gods’ wine on Olympus

name: Laomedon
tagline: Cheated two gods and a hero, and paid for all three.
story: Son of Ilus. Poseidon built the walls of Troy for him and Apollo herded his cattle, but when their year was up he sent them away unpaid, and threatened to cut off their ears. Then a sea monster came against Troy. He promised Heracles his divine horses to kill it, and cheated him too. Heracles sacked Troy and killed him with all his sons but one.
versions: Homer knows the sea monster and the horses; Apollodorus and Hyginus add his daughter Hesione, chained by the sea for the monster.

name: Capys
tagline: Father of Anchises.
story: Son of Assaracus, and father of Anchises.

name: Priam
tagline: Fifty sons, and he outlived nearly all of them.
story: Son of Laomedon, and the last king of Troy. He had fifty sons, nineteen of them by Hecuba. When Achilles killed Hector, the old king went alone by night to Achilles’ hut, kissed the hands that had killed his son and begged for the body. When Troy fell, Achilles’ son Neoptolemus killed him at the altar of Zeus.
versions: Apollodorus and Hyginus: as a boy he was called Podarces, the only son of Laomedon that Heracles spared; his sister Hesione bought him free, and he was called Priam, from the word for buying. Pausanias, after Lesches: Neoptolemus dragged him from the altar and killed him at the gate of his palace.

name: Hecuba
tagline: Watched her city fall and her children die, and became a dog.
story: Wife of Priam, and mother of Hector, Paris, Cassandra and many more. Before Paris was born she dreamed she gave birth to a firebrand that burned Troy. When the city fell she was given to Odysseus as a slave. In Euripides she avenged her youngest son by blinding the man who murdered him.
versions: Her father: Dymas in Homer, Cisseus in Euripides.

transformation.text: A dog with fiery eyes, at the end of her life

name: Tithonus
tagline: Given eternal life, but not eternal youth.
story: Son of Laomedon and brother of Priam. Eos, the Dawn, fell in love with him and carried him away. She asked Zeus to make him immortal, but forgot to ask that he stay young. When he grew old and shrivelled, she shut him away in a room, where his voice runs on for ever. By her he had Memnon.

immortal.text: Made deathless at Eos’s asking, but left to grow old for ever

name: Hesione
tagline: Chained by the sea for her father’s debts.
story: Daughter of Laomedon. When Poseidon sent a sea monster against Troy, she was chained on the shore for it to eat, and Heracles killed it. When he later sacked Troy, he gave her to his friend Telamon, and let her buy one brother free: Priam.

name: Anchises
tagline: A cowherd on Ida, loved by Aphrodite.
story: Son of Capys. He was herding cattle on Mount Ida when Aphrodite came to him in the shape of a mortal girl. She bore him Aeneas, and warned him never to tell who the mother was. When Troy fell, Aeneas carried him out of the burning city.

name: Hector
tagline: Fought for a city he knew would fall.
story: Eldest son of Priam and Hecuba, and the greatest fighter of Troy. On the walls he said goodbye to Andromache and their baby son, knowing the city would fall. He killed Patroclus, and Achilles, mad with grief, killed him before the walls and dragged his body behind his chariot. Priam ransomed it, and the Iliad ends with Hector’s funeral.

name: Andromache
tagline: Lost husband, son and city, and served the son of her husband’s killer.
story: Daughter of Eetion, king of Thebe under Mount Placus. Achilles sacked her city and killed her father and her seven brothers. She married Hector and bore him Astyanax. When Troy fell, her son was thrown from the walls and she was given to Neoptolemus, Achilles’ son, as his prize.

name: Cassandra
tagline: Told the truth, and was never believed.
story: The most beautiful of Priam’s daughters. Apollo gave her the gift of prophecy to win her; when she refused him, he made sure no one would believe her. She foretold the fall of Troy in vain. Agamemnon took her home as his prize, and Clytemnestra killed her with him.
versions: In the Iliad and the Odyssey she is only the loveliest of Priam’s daughters. The Cypria has her prophesy; Aeschylus tells how Apollo gave her the gift and spoiled it.

name: Polyxena
tagline: Sacrificed on Achilles’ tomb.
story: Daughter of Priam and Hecuba. After Troy fell, the ghost of Achilles demanded her, and the Greeks cut her throat on his tomb. In Euripides she went to her death willingly, as a free woman, rather than live as a slave.

name: Troilus
tagline: Ambushed by Achilles outside the walls.
story: A young son of Priam, who loved horses. Achilles lay in wait for him outside Troy and killed him in the sanctuary of Apollo.
versions: Apollodorus: some say his father was Apollo, not Priam.

name: Deiphobus
tagline: Married Helen after Paris died, and paid for it.
story: Son of Priam and Hecuba, and Hector’s dearest brother; Athena took his shape to lure Hector into facing Achilles. After Paris died, he married Helen. On the night Troy fell, Menelaus killed him.

name: Aeneas
tagline: Saved by the gods to rule the Trojans after Troy.
story: Son of Anchises and Aphrodite. He fought for Troy, and the gods saved him more than once: Aphrodite and Apollo from Diomedes, Poseidon from Achilles, because he was fated to survive and rule the Trojans. When the city fell, he carried his father out of the flames.

name: Astyanax
tagline: Thrown from the walls of Troy.
story: Son of Hector and Andromache. His father called him Scamandrius; the Trojans called him Astyanax, lord of the city. As a baby he screamed at his father’s plumed helmet. When Troy fell, the Greeks threw him from the walls, so that no son of Hector would grow up to avenge him.

name: Aeacus
tagline: So just he settled quarrels among the gods.
story: Son of Zeus and the nymph Aegina, and king of the island named after her. When plague emptied it, Zeus turned its ants into men, the Myrmidons. He was so just that he settled quarrels even among the gods.

name: Peleus
tagline: Wrestled a goddess, and married her.
story: Son of Aeacus. Zeus and Poseidon both wanted the sea goddess Thetis, until it was foretold that her son would be greater than his father; so she was given to a mortal. She turned into fire, water and wild beasts, but Peleus held on and won her. All the gods came to the wedding. Their son was Achilles.

name: Thetis
tagline: Married to a mortal against her will, and outlived her son.
story: A sea goddess, daughter of the old man of the sea, Nereus. She was married to the mortal Peleus against her will. She tried to burn away her baby’s mortality in the fire, and when Achilles went to Troy, she rose from the sea to comfort him, knowing he would die young.

transformation.text: Fire, water and wild beasts, struggling in Peleus’s arms

name: Achilles
tagline: Chose a short life and undying fame.
story: Son of Peleus and the goddess Thetis. He was offered a long life without fame or a short one with undying glory, and chose glory. At Troy he quarrelled with Agamemnon and stayed out of the fighting, until Hector killed his friend Patroclus. Then he killed Hector and dragged the body behind his chariot, until Priam came to beg for it. He died by an arrow of Paris, guided by Apollo.
versions: Homer only foretells his death at the hands of Paris and Apollo. Apollodorus: the arrow struck his ankle.

name: Neoptolemus
tagline: Killed an old king at an altar, and died at one himself.
story: Son of Achilles, brought to Troy after his father died. He was one of the men in the Wooden Horse. When the city fell he killed Priam at the altar of Zeus, and took Andromache as his prize. He married Hermione, Menelaus’s daughter, who had been promised to Orestes, and was killed at Delphi.
versions: Who killed him at Delphi: in Euripides, the Delphians, stirred up by Orestes; in Apollodorus, Orestes, or a Delphian named Machaereus; in Pindar, a man in a quarrel over the sacrificial meat.
